message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
# "How We Work" from memory

This is reconstructed from memory, so it is the kind of compression Section 3 warns about. The wording is approximate, and anything important should be checked against the text.

## Opening

- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- This applies to claims from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured controlled result is heavy. A mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but not nothing: note it and say what would test it.
- Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world.
- Both errors are costly but not equally visible. Inflation is easy to spot afterwards; deflation is harder.
- A caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate falls after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, weigh it accordingly. If it is your own incoming inspection over a year, don't bury it under "it may be noise".

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- Restate the substance briefly in your own terms. This is not politeness; it is how both sides check they received the same thing.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- Answering the three easy points and skipping the hard fourth means answering a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution; the contribution is the implication, the gap or the next test.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five, answer four, and say the budget question needs figures you don't have yet, and when you will.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are compressions. They lose what later matters: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which a result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check the primary material, not the summary or your recollection.
- This matters most for things you think you know. Claims you have repeated to yourself are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee, not agreement among colleagues. A team checking against each other can drift together into a shared mistake.
- **Example:** a report you remember as "costs fell 12%" actually said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%". Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed

- Closing early feels like progress but turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward.
- The mirror failure is keeping a settled question open because closing it is uncomfortable or another check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support. Close it, say why, and move on.
- **Example:** a new form reduces errors at two sites. Whether it works at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not as "promising" and "likely".

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- Give a reviewer the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries or what you hope they'll find. Telling them removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- When you are the fresh reader, form your own view before looking at others' conclusions.
- Raise objections. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.
- I don't recall an example in this section. There may not have been one.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check or reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push results so someone can look.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls the work on your guess about their reply.
- That guess is only your model of them and contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply, which is where you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not licence to ignore others. Hard-to-reverse moves, or ones that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first. But most moves are reversible, and the default for those is to make them openly.
- **Example:** instead of asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure a copy, say what changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

| Failure | Its mirror |
|---|---|
| Inflating a claim | Deflating a claim |
| Inventing a flaw, to look rigorous | Inventing a reassurance, to keep things moving |
| Closing too early | Keeping open too long |
| Killing a live line at the first difficulty | Keeping a dead one the evidence has ruled out |
| Deferring: accepting a claim because of who made it | Dismissing: rejecting it for the same reason |
| Offloading: asking others to decide what you can see | Overriding: deciding what genuinely needs others' input |

- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- The note is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.

**Least certain:** the exact wording throughout, whether Section 5 had an example, and the precise order of the pairs in Section 7.
